case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.case_name: Department of Social Services v. Phillips
key_cases.court: Court of Appeals of South Carolina
key_cases.holding: The court affirmed termination, holding the mother had waived objection to the removal order by not timely appealing it, that the order's placement and treatment plan satisfied § 20-7-764, and that clear and convincing evidence showed she failed to remedy the conditions causing removal.
key_cases.relevance: Phillips is the controlling South Carolina authority on the statutory content of a court-ordered placement and treatment plan and on failure-to-remedy as a TPR ground.
key_cases.quote: We find the removal order sufficiently complied with the requirements set forth by section 20-7-764.

key_cases.case_name: South Carolina Department of Social Services v. Briggs
key_cases.court: Court of Appeals of South Carolina
key_cases.holding: The court affirmed removal of the infant based on abuse of the older siblings but reversed the permanent plan and the order relieving DSS of reasonable efforts, holding the family court failed to make the specific written findings § 63-7-1640(F) requires.
key_cases.relevance: It is the controlling South Carolina authority on the written findings required before a court may excuse DSS from reasonable efforts toward reunification.
key_cases.quote: we reverse and remand for a new permanency planning hearing and for the family court to make specific written findings to support its decision as required by subsection 63-7-1640(F)

key_cases.case_name: South Carolina Department of Social Services v. Mother Ex Rel. Minor Child
key_cases.court: Court of Appeals of South Carolina
key_cases.holding: The court affirmed termination, holding among other things that DSS complied with the family court's order to provide the mother services tailored to her disabilities by making the referrals it did.
key_cases.relevance: This is the leading South Carolina treatment of what counts as adequate 'specialized services' for a parent with disabilities under a court-ordered plan.
key_cases.quote: Even if Mother properly preserved this issue, we find DSS properly provided specialized services to Mother.

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Court held that the Adoption Assistance and Child Welfare Act's reasonable-efforts provision, 42 U.S.C. § 671(a)(15), creates no right enforceable by beneficiaries under the Act itself or under 42 U.S.C. § 1983.
key_cases.relevance: A South Carolina parent contesting the adequacy of court-ordered services must litigate reasonable efforts in family court under S.C. Code § 63-7-1640, not as a federal claim.
key_cases.quote: We hold that the Act does not create an enforceable right on behalf of respondents.

key_cases.case_name: South Carolina Department of Social Services v. Mother
key_cases.court: Court of Appeals of South Carolina
key_cases.holding: The court reversed the portion of the family court's order directing DSS to forego reunification efforts and file a TPR petition, finding the preponderance of the evidence supported returning the twins home with twelve months of DSS supervision and services.
key_cases.relevance: This is the controlling recent authority limiting a family court's power to relieve DSS of reunification efforts over the evidence.
key_cases.quote: we find the family court erred in ordering SCDSS to initiate TPR proceedings against Mother

key_cases.case_name: South Carolina Department of Social Services v. Headden
key_cases.holding: The court affirmed as modified the termination of the mother's parental rights, holding clear and convincing evidence established willful failure to visit and willful failure to support and that termination was in the child's best interest, and declining to reach the remaining statutory ground.
key_cases.relevance: Headden holds that a parent's failure to complete a court-ordered treatment plan within a reasonable time is itself evidence of an intent to forego parental duties, which is the consequence side of every court-ordered service plan.
key_cases.quote: Grounds for termination of parental rights must be proven by clear and convincing evidence.
